raw_case_text:
A 76-year-old female patient presented to the department of oral pathology and microbiology with a chief complaint of difficulty in eating for the past 1 week. The patient also gave a history of pain in the upper right back tooth region for 8 months, following which extraction was performed due to the presence of periodontally compromised 16 and 17, after which the symptoms were temporarily relieved. On intraoral examination, a well-defined lesion approximately 2.5 cm x 1.5 cm in size with everted and slightly indurated margins was present on the edentulous alveolar ridge with respect to missing 16 and 17, which was extending to the vestibule. There were no symptoms of nasal regurgitation, but the patient presented with a nasal twang.
The patient was diabetic and was under medication for the past 8 months after extraction was done. Bilateral submandibular lymph nodes were slightly enlarged and mobile. Orthopantomogram showed irregular alveolar bone loss. Water's view depicted slight haziness in the right maxillary sinus and bone loss in the involved area. The patient complained of discomfort in the same region for the past 7 days and also submitted a piece of tissue which had been dislodged from the upper left back tooth region while eating. The tissue was immediately preserved, subjected to decalcification, processed and then histopathologically examined.
The decalcified sections of the hard tissue bit received showed abundant bony trabeculae with empty osteocytic lacunae, absence of osteoblastic rimming and prominent resting and reversal lines. Numerous fungal hyphae and spores of varying morphology were seen in the marrow spaces. Some fungal hyphae were broad, aseptate and ribbon shaped, showing branching at obtuse angles representing Mucorales species, whereas others were thin and septate, showing branching at acute angles representing Aspergillus species [Figure 1]. Fungal spores of varying sizes were observed, exhibiting budding at some places along with fruiting bodies of Aspergillus [Figure 1]. These were easily identified as Aspergillus niger and Aspergillus flavus.
Numerous actinomycotic colonies were also noted along with other bacterial colonies, including both bacilli and cocci arranged in clusters as well as individually in close association with peripheral bony trabeculae [Figure 1]. Focal areas showed chronic inflammatory cell infiltrate comprising lymphocytes. A few small blood vessels, extravasated RBCs, areas of necrosis and vegetable matter were observed. Grocott's methenamine silver staining showed septate Aspergillus hyphae, aseptate Mucorales hyphae and fungal spores along with actinomycotic colonies [Figures 2-5]. The final diagnosis was given as chronic osteomyelitis associated with a combination of mucormycosis, aspergillosis and actinomycosis.

subjective.chief_complaint: A 76-year-old diabetic female presented with a 1-week history of difficulty eating, right maxillary discomfort, nasal speech, and spontaneous dislodgement of a necrotic bone fragment from the posterior maxilla while eating.
subjective.history_of_present_illness: Eight months prior to presentation, the patient underwent extraction of periodontally compromised upper right molars (teeth 16 and 17) after experiencing 8 months of localized dental pain, and was started on oral antidiabetic medication. One week prior to presentation, she developed difficulty eating, right posterior maxillary discomfort, a nasal twang without nasal regurgitation, and brought in a piece of necrotic bone tissue that had spontaneously dislodged from her posterior maxilla while eating.
subjective.past_medical_history: Diabetes mellitus on oral medication for the past 8 months; dental extraction of upper right first and second molars (16 and 17) 8 months prior.
subjective.review_of_systems: Positive for difficulty eating (1 week), right maxillary discomfort, nasal speech (twang), and spontaneous oral bone sequestration; negative for nasal regurgitation.

objective.physical_examination: Extraoral exam revealed slightly enlarged, mobile bilateral submandibular lymph nodes. Intraoral exam showed a well-defined 2.5 x 1.5 cm ulcerated lesion with everted, slightly indurated margins on the edentulous right maxillary alveolar ridge (missing teeth 16 and 17) extending into the buccal vestibule, accompanied by a nasal twang.
objective.routine_investigations: Orthopantomogram (OPG) demonstrated irregular maxillary alveolar bone loss, and Waters' sinus radiograph showed haziness of the right maxillary sinus with adjacent alveolar bone destruction.
objective.advanced_workup: Histopathological examination of the decalcified exfoliated maxillary bone sequestrum (H&E and Grocott methenamine silver [GMS] stains) revealed necrotic bony trabeculae with empty osteocytic lacunae, absent osteoblastic rimming, prominent reversal lines, and marrow spaces packed with three distinct groups of organisms: (1) thin septate fungal hyphae branching at acute angles with fungal spores and characteristic Aspergillus fruiting bodies (conidial heads) identified morphologically as Aspergillus niger and Aspergillus flavus; (2) broad, ribbon-like aseptate hyphae branching at obtuse/right angles characteristic of Mucorales; and (3) numerous basophilic filamentous actinomycotic colonies alongside mixed coccal and bacillary bacterial clusters.

assessment_and_plan.assessment_and_confirmation: Chronic maxillary osteomyelitis caused by a rare triple polymicrobial co-infection with aspergillosis (Aspergillus niger and Aspergillus flavus), mucormycosis (Mucorales), and actinomycosis in a 76-year-old diabetic patient following dental extraction, definitively confirmed by H&E and Grocott methenamine silver histopathology of the exfoliated maxillary bone sequestrum.
